To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
tables are a form of communication, that there is a need to process tables, and that we do not yet understand tables well enough to process them effectively.

(1) tables have a logical structure and a physical structure, and the two are not the same; (2) tables can be represented as a set of rows, columns, and cells, and the cells can be represented as sets of rows, columns and values;

the most important research issue is the design of a table representation that is both human- and computer-readable, that the most important application is the automatic update of databases, that the most significant research challenge is to find the optimal level of abstraction at which tables should be processed, and that the most significant application of tables in the future will be in multimedia information systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of algorithms that enable us to extract the logical structure from the physical structure of tables.
the development of algorithms and systems that will enable us to use tables in new and powerful ways.
the development of algorithms for table processing, and the development of formal models for table structures, and we need both.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the field has made significant progress in the last few years, but there is a long way to go.
we know a lot about what we don’t know about tables, and that there is still much to be done.
the field has not yet achieved a satisfactory understanding of what tables are, how to represent them, and how to use them.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are not yet ready for a “table revolution,” but we are getting close.
there are many ways to process tables, and that the best way is yet to be found.
we know what we do not know.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the research issues in table processing are not as simple as they first appear.
a table is not just a table, and that the design of table processing systems should take into account the intended uses of the table, the nature of the source material, and the intended users.
there are significant differences between tables that are designed for display and tables that are intended for data entry.
